questions.q: Why do portfolio weights drift away from their target even with zero trading?
options: Different assets earn different returns, so their dollar values grow at different rates, changing their relative weights purely from price movement
Weights only drift if the portfolio manager makes a mistake
Weights never actually drift without explicit trades
Drift only happens if the target weights were wrong to begin with
questions.explain: No trading is required for weights to drift -- differing returns alone change each asset's dollar value and therefore its weight in the portfolio.

questions.q: What distinguishes band (threshold) rebalancing from calendar rebalancing?
options: Band rebalancing trades only when a weight drifts beyond a pre-set tolerance, while calendar rebalancing trades on a fixed schedule regardless of how far weights have drifted
They are mathematically identical strategies
Calendar rebalancing never actually trades
Band rebalancing requires more trades than calendar rebalancing in all cases
questions.explain: Calendar rebalancing is time-triggered; band rebalancing is drift-triggered -- it only acts when weights actually move far enough to matter.

questions.q: In the simulation, the 3%-band rule achieved a LOWER maximum tracking error (6.83%) than monthly calendar rebalancing (8.54%) while using fewer rebalances (7 vs. 12). What does this demonstrate?
options: A fixed calendar schedule can let drift run unchecked between scheduled dates, while a band rule rebalances precisely when drift actually warrants it
Calendar rebalancing is always worse than band rebalancing in every possible scenario
This result must be a simulation error, since more rebalances should always produce lower tracking error
Band rebalancing and calendar rebalancing always produce identical results
questions.explain: Calendar rebalancing sometimes trades when drift is small (wasted turnover) and sometimes lets drift run between scheduled dates; band rebalancing reacts directly to drift, which can be both more effective and cheaper.

questions.q: Widening the rebalancing band from 3% to 5% cut turnover by about 75% but raised average tracking error from 3.32% to 4.85%. What does this illustrate?
options: A real, measurable tradeoff between trading costs (turnover) and staying close to target (tracking error) -- not a free lunch in either direction
Wider bands always improve both turnover and tracking error simultaneously
Band width has no measurable effect on portfolio behavior
Turnover and tracking error are unrelated to each other
questions.explain: Widening the band reduces how often you trade (lower turnover, lower cost) at the price of tolerating more drift from target (higher tracking error) -- a genuine tradeoff, not something you can improve on both axes for free.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say there is no universally correct band width or calendar frequency for rebalancing?
options: The right choice depends on each asset's trading costs, the portfolio's size, and how much tracking error the investor is actually willing to tolerate
Regulations set a single required rebalancing frequency for all portfolios
Rebalancing frequency has no actual effect on portfolio performance
The optimal band width is always exactly 3%
questions.explain: The turnover-vs-tracking-error tradeoff depends on real, portfolio-specific inputs (trading costs, size, tolerance for drift) -- there's no single number that's right for every portfolio.
